opus-5.5.text:
I think there's a lot of truth to it, though I'd say "historical accident" is only half the story. Many of the components we treat as standard were introduced for a specific reason, in a specific setting, under the constraints of the time. Someone was training on a certain dataset, with a certain amount of compute, and a certain optimizer, and they found something that worked. Then it gets into a successful architecture, everyone copies that architecture, and after a few years nobody asks why it's there anymore. It becomes the default.

Take normalization, or the choice of activation function, or even small things like how you downsample at the start of a network. When we worked on ConvNeXt, a big part of the exercise was exactly this. We took a standard ResNet and asked what happens if we question these inherited design choices one at a time: the stage ratios, the kernel sizes, using fewer activations and normalization layers, swapping BatchNorm for LayerNorm. Each one was a fairly modest change, but together they brought a pure ConvNet up to the level of hierarchical vision transformers. That told us a lot of what people credited to the transformer paradigm wasn't only about attention. Some of it was about accumulated design decisions and better training recipes that the older architectures simply hadn't been revisited with.

But I wouldn't call these components arbitrary. Residual connections and normalization survived because they solve real problems, especially in optimization. Something can be accidental in its exact form and still be capturing something essential. The accident is often in the specifics: why this particular formula, why this placement, why this ratio. We may have landed on one point in a much bigger design space, and it worked well enough that we stopped searching.

So my view is that we should keep a healthy skepticism. When a component is in every model, that's evidence it's useful, but it's not proof that it's optimal or even necessary, particularly as conditions change. Components designed for one scale of data and compute may not be the right ones today. It's always worth asking: if we were designing this from scratch now, knowing what we know, would we still end up with the same thing? Often the answer is probably not, and that's where some of the most interesting research opportunities are.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Ravid. I actually think that framing is largely right, and it's something I've thought about a lot, partly because of my own work on things like ConvNeXt and on simplifying architectures.

If you look at how most of the standard components came to be, they weren't derived from first principles. Someone tried something on the hardware and the benchmark that was available at the time, it worked a bit better, and it stuck. Batch normalization is a good example. It was introduced for a particular training setup with a particular batch size regime, and then it became a default that people didn't question for years. The same with max pooling, or the specific choice of ReLU, or the exact placement of the normalization layer relative to the residual connection. Each of those had a reasonable motivation when it was introduced, but the reason it survived is mostly inertia. People build on the thing that already works, and the component gets inherited by every subsequent architecture without anyone re-asking whether it's still necessary.

What convinced me of this most strongly was the ConvNeXt project. We took a standard ResNet and, step by step, modernized it with design choices that had been popularized by Vision Transformers: fewer normalization layers, GELU instead of ReLU, larger kernels, layer norm instead of batch norm, and so on. And you could basically recover the performance of a Transformer with a pure convolutional network. That told me two things. First, a lot of the gap between architecture families was about these accumulated small decisions, not about some fundamental advantage of attention. And second, many of the components we thought were essential to a ConvNet were just artifacts of when ConvNets were designed.

That said, I'd push back a little on taking "historical accident" too far. Some things persist because they genuinely are robust. Residual connections, for instance, have survived every architecture shift, and I think that's because they address a real optimization problem that doesn't go away. So I'd say the right attitude is not that everything is arbitrary, but that every component deserves to be re-examined under current conditions: current scale, current data, current hardware. The components that survive that re-examination are probably not accidents. The ones that don't were.

And practically, I think this matters for how we do research. If you treat the standard architecture as a given, you'll tune around it. If you treat it as a pile of contingent decisions, you start doing ablations that actually remove things rather than only add things, and that's where a lot of the interesting simplifications come from. Some of my recent work on normalization-free Transformers comes from exactly that mindset: just asking whether a component we all assume is required can be replaced by something much simpler.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s some truth to that, but I would be careful with the word “accident.” An architecture component might have been a very reasonable choice when it was introduced, given the compute, datasets, and training methods available at the time. Then it becomes standard, and we keep using it even as those conditions change.

The interesting question is whether we still need it today. That’s an empirical question. You can remove a component or replace it with something simpler, but you have to give that alternative a fair chance—you may need to adjust the training recipe, rather than just drop it into a system tuned for the original architecture.

So I view established architectures as good starting points, not as something inevitable. Understanding which choices are essential and which are inherited conventions can help us build simpler models, and also understand why they work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s some truth to that, although I wouldn’t say they’re purely accidents. An architecture component is usually developed in a particular context—with a particular dataset, compute budget, and training recipe. It works well, other people adopt it, and eventually it becomes something we take for granted. But the conditions that made it useful may have changed.

So I think it’s valuable to revisit those choices. If you remove a component and train carefully, do you actually lose anything? Sometimes you do, and that tells you it’s serving an important purpose. Sometimes you don’t, which suggests that the original justification may no longer apply. That doesn’t make the original decision wrong. It just means we should treat architecture design as a set of hypotheses we can test, rather than a collection of rules we have to preserve.
